dod_intent_evidence: Own-site language explicitly names military platforms as a target market ('critical actuation systems for commercial aviation and defense'; separate 'Defence' page in nav) — but the only evidenced production contract to date (Reuters/AeroOnline news) is 100% commercial (Aviointeriors business-class seats), so the DoD motion is real but still aspirational, not yet a named defense customer.
score_evidence: "10x faster lead times... up to 10x reductions in cost and lead time for certifiable products" — business/speed claims, not lab-spec bragging → lab_language_intensity kept low

"We develop and certify our core motor control software to DO-178C standards as a modular, reusable library" — fluent in FAA/aviation certification but zero mention of DDIL/ATO/RMF/CMMC/ITAR anywhere despite naming military platforms as a market → deployment_awareness_absence

"Salient Motion designs, manufactures, and supports advanced electromechanical actuation systems for both commercial and military platforms" — no operator, warfighter, training, or CONOPS language anywhere in the pack → operator_absence
Open roles include a Quality Manager but no field/deployment/compliance/ISSO role tied to defense accreditation → hiring_profile_skew

"Salient Motion said on Wednesday it had secured its first production contract" (Feb 2026) against "$4,000,000... Seed Round (2024-10-01)" — fresh seed, first-ever production win, tiny team → stage_pressure

blind_spots.blind_spot: DO-178C is aviation software certification (FAA-lineage), not a DoD authority-to-operate — the company treats 'certification-centric engineering' as solved without addressing that military platforms require separate RMF/CMMC accreditation.
blind_spots.operator_reality: A DO-178C-certified actuator can be airworthy and still be years from an ATO on a DoD network or program; conflating the two is exactly the kind of assumption that stalls a defense transition even after the engineering is done.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Team's certification playbook was built for the commercial aviation customers they've actually closed (Aviointeriors), then generalized to 'military platforms' without a distinct DoD compliance narrative.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: "Our systems are designed with certification in mind from day one. All reusable components follow a strict design assurance process, enabling rapid safety case development and up to 10x reductions in cost and lead time for certifiable products."

blind_spots.blind_spot: 'Forward-deployed engineers' is pitched as premium customer support for OEMs and MROs, with no mention of spares, power/battery logistics, or field-repair training for an actuator that fails on a fielded military platform at an austere site.
blind_spots.operator_reality: A commercial-aviation support model (call the vendor, get an engineer flown out) does not survive contact with an OCONUS operating environment where the actuator failure has to be fixed by the E-5 on hand, not a company engineer on a plane.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The support model is built around their one evidenced customer type — commercial OEMs/MROs with normal logistics access — not a deployed military unit.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: "We're always ready to go above and beyond for our customers, including providing forward-deployed engineers as needed."

blind_spots.blind_spot: No prime/flow-down or advocacy-chain language anywhere — the entire go-to-market pitch is a commercial supply-chain disruption story (faster/cheaper than legacy suppliers) with zero discussion of how a two-year-old actuator supplier gets qualified onto an existing DoD platform.
blind_spots.operator_reality: Getting designed into a fielded military aircraft or ground system typically runs through a prime integrator's qualification process and GFE integration — a story about beating OEM markup on price doesn't address who champions them past that gate, and their only closed deal so far is commercial.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The founding team's pitch (ex-Anduril engineers per Reuters) leans on manufacturing speed and cost as the wedge, which is a real differentiator for commercial aviation but doesn't map to how DoD platform integration actually happens.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: "We provide high-quality, certified actuation solutions without the overhead costs of legacy providers. By offering competitive pricing and transparent support, we empower OEMs and MROs with true choice in the marketplace."

opener_hook: Salient's actuator software is DO-178C certified for commercial aircraft — is there a separate ATO path mapped for the military platforms on the roadmap?
what_they_do: Designs and manufactures certified electromechanical actuation systems (with a software-first, DO-178C-certified control architecture) for commercial aircraft and, per their site, military platforms.
